articles.title: Persistence of force
articles.content: WHILE the Balochistan insurgency has been simmering for many decades, in recent years, it seems to be spinning out of control. In July this year, Balochistan became the country’s most violent province, replacing KP for the first time. Some sources say there were 176 terrorist attacks, killing 438 people, including 127 security personnel, the highest ever in a month. This consistent increase in the insurgency’s lethality and spread implies a major mismatch between the threat and the measures taken to counter it. One major weakness is the imbalance between using armed force to address the challenge and subordinating the political dimension that sustains it. This begs the question: why do we continue to rely totally on the use of force to combat this insurgency, knowing that it has not worked for decades? Historically, COIN (counter-insurgency) strategies have succeeded only when they struck the right balance between armed force and political measures. At best, force can create the right conditions to end an insurgency, but only politics can use that opening to bring about peace through negotiations. In fact, David Galula, in his book Counterinsurgency Warfare: Theory and Practice, argues that a successful COIN strategy is “80 per cent political and 20pc military”. His “First Law of COIN” is that “the support of the population is as necessary for the counterinsurgent as the insurgent”, and that this support can be achieved only through political measures. Similarly, Rupert Smith, in his book The Utility of Force: The Art of War in the Modern World, defines insurgency as “a war amongst people”. He points out the strategic error of using armed force in an insurgency in a way that alienates the local population, reducing the utility of the force used. Thus, local support is crucial to maximising the utility of armed force in dealing with an insurgency and giving the counter-insurgents the upper hand. Two broad narratives currently shape the Baloch insurgency. The first one, led by Baloch political leaders like Akhtar Mengal and Dr Abdul Malik Baloch (both heads of political parties and former chief ministers of Balochistan), emphasises that the insurgency in Balochistan is predominantly a political problem and requires a political approach for resolution. The second narrative — the military-led state view — which is being implemented in Balochistan is based on the premise that the Baloch insurgency is essentially sponsored by hostile foreign intelligence agencies, and local grievances are of secondary importance. At a workshop on Balochistan at GHQ last year, the military leadership pointed out that foreign-sponsored proxies continually sought to fuel violence and undermine stability in Balochistan. They would be met with a firm response by the military, it was said. This fundamental difference in the threat assessment of the Baloch insurgency between the establishment and the local political leadership leads to divergent responses. The externalisation of the insurgency in Balochistan explains the state’s predominant use of force. Framing the Baloch insurgency as being solely driven by Indian agencies makes it a part of the broader Pakistan-India hostility, and hence defines it as a security threat and not a political challenge. This narrative, naturally, supports a purely coercive response. Interestingly, as a response to the spike in violence in Balochistan in 2026, the state has responded by adding another command to FC Balochistan — with no concomitant political initiatives. Two broad narratives currently shape the Baloch insurgency. Indeed, there is much weight in the establishment’s assertion regarding external support to the Baloch insurgents, which is backed by solid evidence, such as the arrest of Indian agent Kulbhushan Jadhav. But to say that the insurgency is totally Indian-supported would be downplaying the significance of the local grievances, which sustain it. This makes our existing COIN strategy in Balochistan lopsided. Two factors strengthen the argument that the insurgency is grounded in local conditions. One, the triggers of the first four waves of Baloch insurgency were local — in 1948 (annexation of Kalat), 1958 (setting up of One Unit, which erased Balochistan as a political entity, and the arrest of Khan of Kalat), 1962-69 (continued One Unit centralisation, new cantonments in Marri/ Bugti areas and Ayub Khan’s repression), and 1973-77 (dismissal of the NAP government by Zulfikar Ali Bhutto). Second, the current insurgency wave has been going on for more than 20 years now, and to sustain it, a regular stream of local recruits, leadership, and support networks is needed. Such an elaborate network, working clandestinely, carrying out violent acts and hunted by the state, could not sustain itself without strong local support. That is not to say the state did not try to tap the political dimension. But the endeavour was sporadic, half-hearted, lacked political ownership, and was abandoned too soon. For instance, in 2015, the political and military leadership decided to launch Pur Aman Balochistan — a three-dimensional initiative comprising talks with militants under the leadership of the then chief minister, Dr Malik, some development projects, and an amnesty for certain categories of militants. Dr Malik contacted different leaders, such as Brahmdagh Bugti, and brought back their response. The talks were given up when Dr Malik’s tenure ended the same year. Other parts of this initiative also tapered off because the government showed little interest. Thus, the persistence of the use of force in Balochistan is primarily due to the framing of this insurgency as a proxy war of hostile countries, and not as an expression of local discontent. This threat assessment does not seem to be working. Carl von Clausewitz in On War states: “The most far-reaching act of judgement that any commander has to make is to establish … the kind of war on which they are embarking.” Because we cannot control it with our current strategy, we must review our assessment of the kind of “war amongst people” we are fighting in Balochistan. Is it an exclusively foreign proxy war or the violent response of radicalised, disgruntled elements of Balochistan, exploited by hostile external elements? Today’s answer will determine whether we can resolve the situation or whether it will become a ‘forever insurgency’. The writer is a former police officer who was Nacta’s first national coordinator.
articles.author: Tariq Parvez

articles.title: Partners and equals
articles.content: IT has been nearly a year since I last wrote an opinion piece. This was not really intentional, just a result of a feeling of hopelessness and helplessness that made me question whether writing is an exercise in futility. But recently, I was surprised when an educationist told me that mylast pieceon the threat to the Margalla Hills wildlife corridor, was put up in their school for students to read. I decided then, that I need to return to writing. And what better day to voice my thoughts than today. Oct 16, 2026, marks the 75th death anniversary of Shaheed-i-Millat Liaquat Ali Khan, the first prime minister of Pakistan, the Quaid-i-Azam’s close friend and supporter, and a stalwart of the independence movement. On that fateful day, he left behind his life partner, Ra’ana, and their two sons, Ashraf and Akber, in their home in Karachi, to fly to Rawalpindi to address the nation. His speech was being aired live byRadio Pakistan. He had been told his life was in danger, but he believed that the message he wanted to give was important enough to face the danger head-on. He never got to address the nation — and his written speech was never allowed to be published. To this day, we can only speculate at what he was going to reveal. His assassination created a vacuum in the political and civil life of the newly birthed Pakistan, the plan of those who stood in the shadows, having plotted to acquire this land for themselves. It also upended the lives of his family, but the resilience of his wife, although tested to the limit, helped them to move forward. Reflecting on the way my grandparents lived, and the values they instilled in their children, helps me to engage more deeply with one of the profound spiritual questions of our human existence — what is our purpose on this earth? Their values, courage, independence of thought, and intentions that led to right action, are beacons of hope, not only for me, but also for my younger compatriots searching for their truth. We don’t find this learning in the history taught in our educational institutions or in textbooks. These subjects treat history as a test question needing to be memorised, rather than as the outcome of lived choices, decisions, actions, and consequences. On that fateful day, he left behind his life partner, Ra’ana, and their two sons, Ashraf and Akber, in their home in Karachi, to fly to Rawalpindi to address the nation. Integrating historical record with personal and familial insights into who my grandparents were, has allowed me to better understand them as individuals. We live in interesting times, and so did they, but they bore greater hardships than us. My grandfather was the son of a nawab, yet refused to follow the system, disobeying his father to study at Oxford, much to the horror of the nawab and his courtiers. He joined the independence movement very soon after his return. My grandmother was the only girl in her class at the University of Lucknow where she graduated with an MSc degree in economics. She was a professor in economics when she met and married my grandfather. For him, she changed her religion, and her name. And became his equal partner in the independence movement. Colonial oppression and resistance were a daily affair, as was the burden of responsibility that each carried, when they became founders and role models for their new nation and its beleaguered citizens. Their personalities were moulded by the events of their time — but this moulding led not to the hardening of hearts, nor to an inability to accept adversity. Rather, in each was developed a sense of empathy towards others regardless of their station in life, compassion that resulted in positive action, and the courage and tenacity to stand for what was right and just. After they married in 1933, Liaquat and Ra’ana visited England for their honeymoon and to persuade Mr Jinnah to return, as the time was ripe for independence. On his request, they returned to tour the provinces so that they could describe to Mr Jinnah the state of affairs of the Muslims of India, and did so in such a way that he was persuaded to return from England to lead the Muslim League. Described by the Quaid as his “right-hand man”, Liaquat was appointed by him as the secretary-general of the Muslim League. My grandmother not only advised the party on economic matters but also learned to type so that she could assist my grandfather with his official correspondence. Their marriage flourished as it was based on mutual love, mutual admiration, and mutual support. When Partition occurred, my grandparents left all their wealth behind in India. My grandfather refused to claim any evacuee property until after each migrant to this land had been compensated for what they left behind. The day he died, he owned no property and had a paltry amount of money in his account. On the flip side, they gifted their mansion in Delhi, named Gul-i-Ra’ana, to the government of Pakistan and it remains the residence of the Pakistan high commissioner. Neither of my grandparents sought to keep any wealth or property for themselves. They gave because, in my view, they were living Islam. Their purpose on this earth was clear to them — live full lives in giving to others, love and be loved, have patience, persevere even in the face of the greatest adversity, remain steadfast even though others try to tear you down, and last but not least, trust in Allah to show you the true path. I pray that more of us can live as they did. The writer is a development professional and impact adviser with over 25 years of experience in designing and managing programmes to improve people’s lives.
articles.author: Samia Liaquat Ali Khan

articles.title: GenZ for mangroves
articles.content: MY expository writing class consists of students who will choose one of four interdisciplinary majors: social development studies, politics, philosophy and economics, Asian and Middle Eastern studies, and environmental science. Gen Z has grown up in the shadow of the Covid pandemic; my students are now studying the nightmare of climate change and the ill effects it will have on Pakistan. Recently, they read a report by Waqas Ali Ranjha in this paper on how mangrove cutting for land reclamation in the Korangi creek is putting the environment in danger. The students were horrified to hear how land grabbers have built an illegal dyke in the Korangi Mangrove Forest, next to the Korangi Biodiversity Park that opened just last year. This dyke blocks water from reaching the mangroves, which will die and be cut down by encroachers. The Sindh Forestry Department confirmed this illegal activity, but the matter is sub judice, and the police will not act. Mayor Murtaza Wahab had asked the public for feedback about the Biodiversity Park, so I tasked my students with composing ‘letters to the editor’ — a classic exercise for university students to “compliment, critique, inform, or communicate information” on a topic they’re passionate about. We keep telling these students that they are responsible for finding the solutions to our manmade problems. They know the importance of the mangroves to Karachi’s coastline, protecting it from floods, storms, and rising sea levels. They fear for the destruction of the mangrove’s unique ecosystem, with its birds, animals, and plants that represent the many miracles of the natural world. Alisha Shah writes, “What bothers me is how calculated the whole thing is ... at this rate we’re going to lose a piece of Karachi that we can’t really get back.” Enara Muluk adds, “We already have very little greenery left in Karachi, so we should at least try to protect the mangroves that are still there.” Students are concerned about the loss of forest cover. These students note contradictions in the legal process that benefit criminals and miscreants while harming our natural resources. For example, Ayesha Baig asks smartly, “How come the [sub judice order] only applied to the Sindh Forest Department when it came to the removal of the bunds and not to those who are making those bunds?” She urges the public to act, citing previous activist movements like India’s 1970s Chipko Movement where women villagers hugged trees to stop deforestation; and the Sundarbans Protection Struggles, where activists recommend a combination of local knowledge and smart governance to protect an endangered mangrove forest in Bengal. Some of my students are concerned not just about the environmental impacts of losing the Korangi mangroves, but the livelihoods of fishermen and the resulting economic loss. “Mangroves serve as indispensable ‘nurseries’ for more than 75 per cent of Pakistan’s commercially viable fish, shrimp, and crab species,” writes Faiz Ahmed. “Karachi’s fishing exports are estimated to have a market value around $500 million; a substantial loss in the wildlife population is reflected in these companies’ bottom lines. And the consumers ... have to pay with their wallet as … the price of that once affordable prawn biryani more closely resembles that of a lobster thermidor.” Destroying the mangroves will have adverse effects on Karachi in other ways, too. Mangroves entrap carbon dioxide, especially relevant in Korangi where factories pollute the air. “If we destroy mangrove ecosystems,” writes Hasnat Alam, “the stored greenhouse gases will be released back into the air. This also weakens Karachi’s ability to [withstand] pollution and to cool the city from heat islands, and it makes urban life less pleasant overall.” But what should be done about this particular disaster unfolding in slow motion before us? The students want the illegal bund to be removed immediately, despite the sub judice order. Muhammed Ayaz says, “Legal disputes should be resolved through proper judicial procedures, but they should not become an excuse for irreversible environmental damage.” Shah Sarbaz Ali Rehmat writes that the authorities must “disclose the Environmental Impact Assessment for this activity, and designate Korangi Creek as a protected zone”. Meanwhile, Fatima Rubi advises the use of satellite technology and community-based monitoring to look for changes in the mangrove cover. I can’t think of anyone who would disagree with Syed Riaz Hussein’s call to action: “Stop the cutting, stop the landfilling, and let the water flow back to the mangroves so they can survive and natural life can be sustained.” Hopefully, the mayor, the Sindh Forestry Department, and the police can be convinced to act fast before the damage is done. After all, as Muhammed Ayaz writes, prevention is preferable to restoration. The writer teaches Expository Writing at AKUFAS.
articles.author: Bina Shah

articles.title: Supreme myth
articles.content: IN the earliest cosmologies, the earth was thought to be at the centre of the universe, Stephen Hawking explains in A Brief History of Time, and the sun and all the planets, stars, and other celestial bodies were believed to revolve around it. This myth of ‘geo-centrism’ or ‘Ptolemaic systems’ would be shattered by the findings of Nicolaus Copernicus in the 16th century — in much the same way, the myth that, following the 27th Amendment, the Supreme Court (SC) and the Federal Constitutional Court have been reconstructed as two co-equal courts is demonstrably shattered by the FCC’s jurisdictional assertions. The 1973 Constitution established the SC as the apex court of the land with the final say in all litigation, constitutional or otherwise. The 26th Amendment compromised this position by creating a division within the SC and assigning adjudication of constitutional matters to a specialised constitutional bench. Nevertheless, the SC retained the solemn task of interpreting the Constitution. However, the 27th Amendment effectively stripped the SC of its plenary power to interpret the Constitution and gave it to the newly created FCC. The 27th Amendment militates against the SC’s apex character, now an attribute of its past. Yet proponents of the amendments, including the SC itself, have strived to present ‘a theory of hierarchy’ which depicts the SC and FCC as two co-equal courts with distinct jurisdictions, and no vertical authority of one dominating the other. Such a theory is flawed, much like the myth of ‘geo-centrism’ or ‘Ptolemaic systems’. Following the 27th Amendment, the FCC appears to precede the SC wherever courts are listed in the Constitution. This symbolic precedence is allegorical. The amended Article 189 of the Constitution now explicitly makes the FCC’s decisions binding on all courts in Pakistan, including the SC. In ‘Shahbaz Masih vs ASJ Lahore (2026)’, the FCC held: “The supremacy of constitutional adjudication now vests in this court [the FCC], and all courts, including the Supreme Court of Pakistan, are bound by its pronouncements.” Thus, the myth that no vertical relationship exists between the SC and the FCC is debunked. The myth of co-equal courts has been shattered. Article 175-E (5) of the Constitution declares: “The Federal Constitutional Court may, on its own motion or otherwise, if it considers that the case involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution, call for the record of any case pending before any court and make such order in the case as it thinks fit.” This power is most extraordinary, and unmistakably vertical. In ‘M/S Matracon Pakistan vs Appellate Tribunal for Sales Tax (2026)’, the FCC held that even a case that otherwise falls within the SC’s jurisdiction can be requisitioned, heard, and finally adjudicated by the FCC on the ground that it involves a question of constitutional law. Most recently, the FCC invoked Article 175-E (5) to requisition cases related to Imran Khan from the SC. Conversely, the SC has no such powers, and is unambiguously denuded of the authority to issue reciprocal orders requisitioning cases from the FCC. The German supreme courts are subordinate to the German Federal Constitutional Court, not because an avenue of appeal exists between the two inter se but because, first, the precedents of the latter are binding on the former akin to Article 189, and second, avenues of checks, somewhat akin to Article 175-E (3) and (5), exist in the German Basic Law. South Africa, Spain, Italy, Austria, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Poland, and Portugal all have supreme courts and federal constitutional courts. The former courts are invariably subordinate to the latter, and in legal philosophy — understood at least since the US supreme court’s ruling in ‘Cohen vs Virginia (1821)’ — only such a model can jurisprudentially sustain the entrenched nature of the constitution. The apex nature of the FCC is grounded in the text of the 27th Amendment, and the doctrine of ‘kompetenz-kompetenz’, which allows it to determine, without limitation, the contours of its own jurisdiction. Thus, the continued asserted supremacy of the SC is a ‘supreme myth’, which the court should abandon, rather than embarrass itself. Many myths, even when shattered, are hard to admit, especially when doing so wounds the ego or injures prestige. In 1633, Galileo was subjected to an inquisition and ultimately convicted for teaching Copernicanism, not because the proposed model was astronomically flawed, but because it contradicted scripture and the long-held position of the Catholic Church.
articles.author: Asad-ul-Mulk

articles.title: Deadly classrooms
articles.content: AT LEAST 30 children, most of them younger than 13, and a teacher have died in Peshawar after the roof of their private schoolcollapsedduring morning classes. Dozens more were injured, some critically. The victims had arrived at the Al Khair school expecting an ordinary day. Instead, rescue workers spent hours searching through rubble as parents gathered outside. Police say the building was structurally weak and its roof overloaded with additional construction. The owner has been arrested, while an inquiry is under way. These preliminary findings demand scrutiny. So do reports that concerns about the building’s condition had previously been raised. In June, 14 children died when the roof of a tuition centrecollapsedin Lahore’s Kahna area. Two days later, another schoolroof collapsein Baghbanpura killed an eight-year-old. Three incidents in a few months should be enough to force an examination of the places where Pakistan’s children are taught. Across the country, schools and tuition centres operate in buildings ill-suited to accommodating large numbers of pupils. In crowded urban neighbourhoods, houses are converted into classrooms, sometimes with additional floors, makeshift rooms, and roofs carrying more weight than they were designed to support. Yet questions about construction quality, structural approvals, and inspections are too often left unanswered until a disaster occurs. The Lahore inquiry found that the Kahna tuition centre operated from an unregistered residential house. Peshawar presents a troubling contrast: according to the KP private schools regulator, Al Khair was registered in March, but technical personnel were absent from its inspection. If a school can receive registration without a structural assessment, what assurance does that certificate provide? Investigators must establish whether alterations were authorised, who inspected the premises, and whether warnings were received and ignored. They must also examine the regulators’ role, not merely the decisions of school management. The KP authorities’ decision to establish district-level committees to inspect private school buildings is welcome, but its value will depend on what follows. The committees have been instructed to examine buildings, identify hazards, and submit reports within three days. Authorities must make the findings public, close premises posing danger, and require independent engineering clearance before they reopen. Similar checks are needed across every province, including at tuition centres and schools operating inside residential properties. Building permission, school registration, and periodic safety certification should be linked, with clear responsibility assigned to qualified inspectors. Owners who make dangerous alterations must face consequences, as must officials found to have neglected their duties. Parents should not have to become structural engineers to judge whether their children are safe at school. After so many deaths, another round of condolences and inquiries without enforcement would be an intolerable response.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Diplomatic options
articles.content: AS Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi movement continue to trade fire, and the US-Iran war is locked in a stalemate, regional states continue to stress the need for a diplomatic solution to the conflicts in both theatres. Numerous attempts have been made in the past to find a negotiated off-ramp in both conflicts, but they have met with little success. Regional states know that the alternative to talks — a fully fledged war on both fronts — will bring immeasurable destruction to the Gulf, the Red Sea and the surrounding areas. The need for diplomacy was stressed during Omani Foreign Minister Badr al-Busaidi’s visit to Pakistan on Wednesday. Though the visit was of a bilateral nature, the regional situation was high on the agenda, with Oman’s top diplomat reiterating that “diplomacy is the only way forward”. Both Pakistan and Oman have played integral roles in trying to find a negotiated settlement to the US-Iran dispute, while the sultanate is also a key link between the Saudis and the Houthis. Both Pakistan and Oman know that any further escalation either in the Gulf or in Yemen will destabilise the whole region. With regard to the Yemeni conflict, while Pakistan has pledged to stand “shoulder to shoulder” with Saudi Arabia, the prospect of a long war of attrition involving the kingdom and its allies, and the pro-Iran Houthis, is in no one’s interest. The goal, therefore, should be a renewed ceasefire, which promises Saudi security and an end to the Yemeni civil war. Pakistan, Oman and other regional states should concentrate on achieving this goal. Where Iran is concerned, it is likely that the US will make its next move after the midterm elections in early November. However, media reports that America plans on dropping the ‘mother of all bombs’ on Iranian energy and nuclear sites should be a matter of concern for all. America’s aggression has failed to make Iran capitulate, and it is hard to see what more violence will achieve, other than perpetuating chaos in the region. What is needed is a holistic ceasefire that addresses all fronts — Iran, Yemen, Lebanon — along with a long-term peace between the US and Iran. The US must also refrain from initiating more wars in the Middle East, along with reining in its bloodthirsty ally Israel.
articles.author: Editorial
